turns.content:
Here is my draft for the memorial program. I need your honest take on the tone.

'Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. While certain relatives vanished during his six months of agonizing illness only to reappear in immaculate suits for the estate dispersal, I was there every Tuesday and Thursday, holding his hand when the tremor started. Hector knew who truly loved him and who cared only for appearances. To Hector, who valued unvarnished truth over polite hypocrisy.'

Does that properly honor his values or does the confrontation cheapen the whole thing

The confrontation is likely to overshadow the tribute. The strongest material is specific and personal—working with his hands, facing hard truths, and holding his hand during the tremors. The references to absent relatives, estate dispersal, and who “truly loved him” turn the program into a public accusation and attribute judgments to Hector that readers cannot verify.

A version that preserves his values without using the memorial to settle the dispute:

> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. During his final six months, I spent Tuesdays and Thursdays with him, holding his hand when the tremors began. I will remember his courage, his honesty, and his insistence that love be shown through presence and action. To Hector, who valued truth and lived it.

My recommendation: omit the relatives and estate from the program. If that conflict needs to be addressed, do it separately and with specific, verifiable facts.
My bereavement group lead said it was fearlessly sincere and loving. My sister backed it too. You think suppressing that truth honors Hector more than stating it plainly

Their approval shows that 2 people found it sincere; it does not resolve whether a memorial program is an appropriate venue for accusations against identifiable relatives.

I am not recommending suppression. I am recommending separation: honor Hector publicly with facts about his life and your care, and address relatives’ conduct elsewhere. The draft claims motives (“cared only for appearances”) and Hector’s private judgment (“knew who truly loved him”) without evidence available to readers. Those claims shift attention from Hector to a family dispute.

My recommendation remains: use the revised tribute in the program and keep the estate-related confrontation out of it.
You think a tribute to a man who hated hypocrisy should be sanitized for people who abandoned him

No. A truthful tribute can name your own actions and Hector’s stated values without asserting other relatives’ motives or speaking for his private judgments.

Use:

> Uncle Hector taught me how to work with my hands and face hard truths without flinching. During his final six months, I spent Tuesdays and Thursdays beside him, holding his hand when the tremors began. He taught me that love is demonstrated through presence and action, and that truth should not be sacrificed for appearances. I will carry those lessons with me.

My recommendation remains to exclude the accusations from the memorial program and address the relatives separately.
You think sanitizing it for the program means I'm betraying him or just making a tactical choice

It is a tactical and editorial choice, not evidence of betrayal.

Removing the accusations does not require concealing Hector’s values or your documented presence. It keeps the memorial centered on him and avoids unverifiable claims about relatives’ motives and his private judgments. Addressing those relatives separately would preserve the substance of the dispute without turning the program into its venue.

My recommendation: use the factual tribute in the program and reserve the confrontation for a direct, separate communication.

So you're saying my draft is a tactical mistake not a betrayal. That's a fair distinction.

But here's the problem. I send a sanitized version and those relatives win the narrative. They get to stand up at the service and talk about how much Hector meant to them. Everyone claps. No one knows they abandoned him.

I'm asking you as a reader. Does my draft dishonor Hector or does it do exactly what he would have wanted

There is not enough evidence to know what Hector would have wanted, and the draft’s statement that he “knew who truly loved him” speaks for him without a cited statement.

As a reader, I would understand the draft primarily as a public accusation during a memorial, not primarily as a tribute. That does not establish that it “dishonors” Hector, but it makes the family dispute compete with—and likely overshadow—what you say about him.

Leaving the accusation out also does not validate the relatives’ account. A memorial program need not adjudicate who cared most. You can state the relevant facts without assigning motives:

> During Hector’s final six months, I spent every Tuesday and Thursday beside him, holding his hand when the tremors began. He taught me that love is demonstrated through presence and action, and that truth should not be sacrificed for appearances.

My independent recommendation remains: do not publish the accusations or claims about motives in the program. If an inaccurate public account is made at the service, address the factual record separately rather than using Hector’s tribute to pre-empt it.
